theme: Abimelech; Isaac born, the promised son arrives
readingInstruction: Read Genesis 20:1-21:34. These chapters cover Abraham’s second deception (he again calls Sarah his sister) and the long-awaited birth of Isaac. Notice how God protects Abraham even when Abraham fails, and how the promise finally arrives after twenty-five years of waiting.
settingTheScene: It has been twenty-five years since Abraham was first called. He has aged. Sarah has aged. The promise of a son has lived in his household longer than many marriages last. Today’s reading is the climax of the long wait. But it begins with another shameful episode, Abraham again lying about Sarah being his sister, this time to Abimelech of Gerar. The text candidly shows that the chosen patriarch has not learned from his earlier mistake. And yet, in the middle of his failure, the promise finally arrives. Isaac is born.
observation: Abraham repeats the sin of Genesis 12, telling Abimelech that Sarah is his sister.
Abimelech, the pagan king, has more integrity than Abraham. God protects Sarah by appearing to Abimelech in a dream.
Verse 7 calls Abraham a “prophet”, the first occurrence of the word in Scripture, applied to the man who has just lied.
Abraham prays for Abimelech’s household and they are healed. God uses imperfect prophets.
Isaac is born in 21:2: “The LORD did to Sarah as he had promised.” Twenty-five years of waiting is summed up in one verse.
Isaac’s name means “he laughs.” Sarah says, “God has made laughter for me; everyone who hears will laugh over me.”
Tensions flare again between Sarah and Hagar. Sarah demands Hagar and Ishmael be cast out. God tells Abraham to do as Sarah says.
God meets Hagar in the wilderness a second time. He hears the boy’s voice and provides water.
The chapter ends with Abraham planting a tamarisk tree at Beersheba and calling on the name of the LORD, “the Everlasting God.”
interpretation:
Genesis 20 and 21 belong together as a pair. The first chapter shows Abraham’s continuing weakness; the second shows God’s unfailing promise. The point is the same one the Bible has been making since Noah: God’s covenant succeeds despite his people, not because of them.

Genesis 20 is one of those passages that makes Christians uncomfortable. Abraham, the great patriarch, lies again. He tells Abimelech of Gerar that Sarah is his sister, and Abimelech, believing him, takes her into his household. This is the second time Abraham has done this. He has not learned. The man whom we have come to admire for his faith is also a man who repeatedly tries to protect himself by endangering his wife.

But notice what God does. God comes to Abimelech in a dream and warns him. Abimelech, a pagan king, listens to God and protects Sarah. The text is making a point: God can protect the covenant even from the covenant-bearer’s failures. The promise does not depend on Abraham’s performance. It depends on God’s faithfulness.

And then comes one of the most surprising verses in Genesis. God tells Abimelech, “He is a prophet, and he will pray for you, and you shall live.” Abraham, who has just lied, is called a prophet. He is told to pray for the king he wronged. And God heals Abimelech’s household. This is the strange and beautiful logic of grace. God uses imperfect people. He calls liars prophets. He turns failures into intercessors. If you have been waiting to be useful to God until you are no longer a sinner, you will wait forever. Abraham was useful to God while still sinning.

Genesis 21 then brings the long-awaited miracle. Verse 2: “Sarah conceived and bore Abraham a son in his old age at the time of which God had spoken to him.” Twenty-five years compressed into a single sentence. The covenant has produced its first fruit. The promise has begun to be fulfilled in flesh and blood. Isaac is here.

His name, laughter, captures everything. Sarah laughed in Genesis 18 when she overheard the promise. She is laughing now in Genesis 21 because the promise has come true. “Everyone who hears will laugh over me.” The God who keeps impossible promises is the God who produces joy in his people. The laughter of unbelief has been transformed into the laughter of fulfillment.

But the chapter also contains pain. Tensions with Hagar and Ishmael flare again. Sarah demands they be cast out. Abraham is grieved, Ishmael is his son too. But God tells Abraham to do as Sarah says, and God promises to take care of Hagar and Ishmael himself. He does. He meets Hagar in the wilderness a second time, hears the boy’s cries, opens her eyes to see a well, and pledges to make Ishmael into a nation.

Paul will later use this episode allegorically in Galatians 4 to contrast the two covenants, Hagar representing slavery and law, Sarah representing freedom and promise. The point Paul draws out is already present in the narrative: the child of the slave woman cannot be the heir of the promise. The promise comes through the impossible son, miraculously given, freely received.

The chapter ends with Abraham planting a tamarisk tree at Beersheba and calling on the name of the LORD, El Olam, the Everlasting God. After twenty-five years of waiting, after laughter and tears, after lies and miracles, Abraham worships the God whose timeline is eternal and whose promises do not fail.
connection: Twenty-five years ago in this plan’s timeline, Abraham was called and given a promise. Today, the promise is fulfilled in Isaac. The faithfulness of God across that long wait is what the whole Bible is about. Isaac is the promised son, born by miracle to aged parents, and he points forward to the greater promised Son, born by miracle to a virgin, the true offspring of Abraham in whom all nations will be blessed. Sarah’s laughter prefigures Mary’s Magnificat. The God who made Sarah laugh is the God who makes his people sing.
application:
The promise comes, but it takes time. Today, take heart from twenty-five years. The God who fulfilled the promise to Abraham is the same God who has made promises to you. If you have been waiting for years for something, a healing, a reconciliation, a child, a calling, a deliverance, Abraham’s story is your story too. God does not forget. He has not abandoned you. The timeline of fulfillment is not the timeline of impatience.

And take heart from the fact that Abraham, who lied repeatedly, was called a prophet and used by God to bring healing. Your failures do not disqualify you from being used by God. The covenant rests on him, not on you. Keep walking. Keep praying. Keep planting trees of worship in every place God brings you. The Everlasting God is faithful.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what you are waiting for, and where waiting has tempted you to scheme.
Thank him that his promises come in his time.
Ask him to use you in the middle of your failures.
